about it, then, believe me, we would not be here talking about it. It is my understanding
that the Government actually knew about the announcement before the announcement
was going to be made. It had an opportunity to actually take advice prior to the
Remuneration Authority coming forward with its recommendation, but Christmas is not
really a good time to actually make these announcements. So we end up where we are
now.
Again, I think all of us have said how unfortunate it is that we are in this place and
this moment without the true ability to even just give it full attention. It is around
algebra. I mean, I do not know how many people in this House who would stick their
hand up and say they are brilliant mathematicians when it comes to algebra. I am
looking; there is nobody. That is good.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: I am now.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Mr Nash has p ut his hand up. We will be testing Mr Nash in
the dinner hour. And the Minister has said that he has very quickly learnt an awful lot
about algebra —so there you go. I have to admit that I have been upstairs working
through it myself, trying to figure out w hat those letters actually mean. I think what has
been most valuable about the contributions for me, anyway, to date is, one, the
contribution from the first Green Party spokesperson, who asked why we do not
consider splitting this out. Minister, why do we  not consider splitting this out? Let us
put a stop to the 3.5 percent. We all agree that the 3.5 percent is just out of whack and is
not acceptable. Why do we not consider actually splitting it out, then, and taking a
moment? Let us just go back to what w e had before. None of us, that I can pick up, was
gagging for an increase in pay. None of us was lobbying. None of us was trying to
actually get more money because all of us are very aware of people inside our areas who
live on a heck of a lot less, or who  are trying to live on a heck of a lot less than what we
get paid to do our job.
There would be no argument. We would probably not even need to take any more
calls if we actually split that bit out and said: “Stop the 3.5. Go back to what it was prior
to the Remuneration Authority.” And then let us take the next year to put the new
equation, the new criteria, through a select committee process. Let us take some time
and allow this voice of New Zealand —the voice of New Zealand —which we know is
out there, to actually come and submit around a select committee process, because then
we would have an enduring solution, and I think that has been what has been pointed
out by previous speakers as well. We have no doubt that this will come back. We often
get pieces o f legislation that have been pushed through. Let us give the benefit of the
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2303
doubt. You know, the staff who write the legislation are doing their best under time
pressures. There is an outcome that is being desired and it is algebra.
The equation was not right last week so are we sure—are we sure, are we sure—that
the modelling done this week is right? Are we sure that the quarterly employment
survey is the thing that we should be working on? Are we sure that when we say in the
legislation that “the Quarte rly Employment Survey for the public sector average
ordinary time weekly earnings for fulltime -equivalent employees using the change for
the average for the year to June compared with the average for the previous year to
June.” that that is going to give us the outcome that we seek? And what is the outcome
that we seek? What we seek is that we do not want to be treated —I believe this is what
we seek—unduly better than any other New Zealand worker out there. We want to be
treated fairly just as they wish to be treated fairly. I do think that Mr Robertson’s point,
reiterated by Mr Shaw, around the inequality that has grown between the average
worker’s salary or wage and that of chief executive officers has contributed to this issue,
and, yet, we are not addres sing it. I do think that that is something that if we were able
to take more time, we could have a really good look at it. I think this has highlighted
that major issue.
It just struck me that when the National Party member for the Wairarapa spoke last
week, he spoke on a bill where he argued about the need for the capacity for employers
in his area to bring in workers who would work for the dollars they were offering as
opposed to the member for Wairarapa standing and arguing that the employers of the
Wairarapa needed to be supported to be able to pay the dollars the workers required and
the dollars they would take that work for. Too often we are hearing about this. Too
often we are hearing that New Zealanders will not take the job; whereas, in reality, New
Zealanders will not take the job for the pay and conditions that are offered. And then
there is an argument, often from the Government benches, that we therefore must bring
in people to fill those positions that New Zealanders will not take. So I think  it is a valid
statement, a valid comment, that the lower pay scales and the higher pay scales inside
the public sector area of New Zealand have got completely out of kilter.
Are we appropriately attaching our pay to the right criteria, through this bill?  I would
say that there is some mood that perhaps we are not. New Zealand First is also working
to try to get a Supplementary Order Paper into the House—I am not sure how successful
we will be—to make this bill, which is to amend the Remuneration Authority  Act 1977,
cover all the people whom the Remuneration Authority has to consider, not just
members of Parliament. We think that that recognises how out of kilter these payments
have become.
There have been a couple of contributions from the Government benc hes. They have
given the impression that we are voting for a pay cut, and that is not the case. The words
“pay drop” were used by Mr Woodhouse and, I believe, by Ms Dowie and also by Mr
Young in the first contribution, if you go back. They gave the suggest ion that we were
voting to give back money or to have a pay cut. Actually, we are not. We are voting
against an increase that was inappropriate. I just want to be really clear. We are not
being that magnanimous. We are voting against an increase that is in appropriate. I
would not want anybody to think that there are all these shining halos all over the place.
What we have found ourselves in is a situation that reflects a problem in the wider
society. We are not addressing the problem in the wider society an d we know that that
problem affects the lower -paid workers in New Zealand. It affects every other area of
their lives.
New Zealand First is not confident that this bill is going to do anything about that. It
is not part of the criteria. It is not part of the brief. We get it. But maybe, just maybe, if
2304 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015
we could take the first part to select committee, maybe, just maybe, we might be able to
have a conversation about the wider issues. Kia ora.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: In this second reading of the
Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill I just
want to clarify a couple of points raised by me in the first reading. In doing so I agree
with the member opposite, the Hon Annette King, that there is certainly no point in
jawboning the authority. There certainly is not. But as part of this amendment, I believe
that the criteria not only needs to be clear but needs to be fair, in the grand scheme of
things, when we look at the economy in New Zealand and, obviously, globally. As part
of that, I agree with what the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety said. It is
incredibly difficult to make comparisons between an MP’s role and other comparable
roles. What is comparable when you take into account staffing levels, accountability,
skills, and results? That is not necessarily underselling us, either, but it is just incredibly
hard to do when you look at the differences in the roles.
I do believe that aligning us with the public sector, the quarterly employment survey,
and the average salary movements, and bracketing us with those hard- working
individuals and officials who work for the Public Service, is fair. We are experiencing
0.8 percent inflation. As has  been mentioned by the Prime Minister, if any increase is
appropriate, a 1 to 2 percent increase is appropriate in these times, as we are asking our
officials to live within their means and do more on less. With that, I commend this bill
to the House.

items.text: The next call is a split call. Metiria
Turei—5 minutes.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I just want to follow on from my
colleague James Shaw and also to acknowledge the contribution from Grant Robertson
who particularly focused on both inequality and that being the driver of increased pay
and the driver of the concern about it, but als o his, I think, very clear description of the
fact that this change means that the Government is in control of MPs’ pay. That is
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2305
exactly the opposite of what many years of work have led to. It is exactly the opposite
of the last Remuneration Authority bill  that we dealt with in the Government
Administration Committee a couple of years ago, which was designed to give it more
authority over MPs’ pay and allowances. So we are going backwards very quickly here.
I do note that the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety did not answer my
question in his last contribution as to whether the Remuneration Authority (Members of
Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill would constrain MPs’ pay increases. I can
assume only that is because either he does not know, be cause they have not done the
modelling, or he knows that it is essentially the status quo.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: I will address that in my speech.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Well, you had the opportunity, Minister, to address it earlier.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: I didn’t have the time. Sadly, I didn’t have the time.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: You did have the time. It would be good to do so quite soon,
because otherwise there is no assumption we can ma ke, except that the reason why the
Government has chosen the quarterly employment survey as the criterion for the
Remuneration Authority is that it makes no change and that that was politically
palatable to National Party MPs. But actually they do not want  to find any means of
constraining MPs’ pay. I would like to think that that is not the case, but until we see
evidence to the contrary that really is the only assumption we can make.
There was a very good discussion earlier about inequality and the fact that part of the
reason why MPs’ pay is such an issue is that there are massive increases for people who
are being paid high wages, and basically wages are static and going backwards for many
on lower incomes. That is certainly true. The Green Party has been very clear about
policy on that as well. Our Supplementary Order Paper 57, which we are putting
forward today to link MPs’ pay to nominal increases in the median wage, is the one that
we put forward last year, so it has been on the table and available f or the Government to
take up for 12 months now. We have also very clearly set out issues around chief
executive officer pay —for example, the requirement for companies to disclose chief
executive officer salaries more clearly, define them, and provide ratio nale for those pay
increases; to have staff members on the committees that set those chief executive officer
pay increases; to require New Zealand’s large companies to report on the pay ratio
between their highest -paid and lowest -paid staffers; and, to inc lude pay ratios in
Government procurement and for Government agencies.
Pay ratio is a major issue here. It is the increasing gap between those on the lowest
rates and those at the top. We see more information coming out today from the Council
of Trade Unions, describing how those in the top 1 percent have increased their income
by around $100,000 between March 2011 and March 2013, meaning that the increase is
now 9.7 times more than that for the average worker. This is what is being seen daily by
ordinary New Zealanders who are doing their best to get ahead. We have a country of
two halves. The bottom half are static or going backwards, fighting every day to have a
good job and to do their best but still are not getting anywhere. We have the other half
who are slowly moving forward, and then at the very top there is the 1.25 percent who
are moving ahead in leaps and bounds. For as long as MPs attach their salary to those
top levels, we will continue to be part of the problem.
We can solve it. We can be part  of the solution by attaching our salary increases to
the nominal increases in the median wage, which means that we link ourselves to the
bulk of the New Zealand population and we have fair pay increases, based on a criterion
that is not determined by Gove rnment but determined by our overall approach to our
economic and social policy. That is where the Green Party would like to see this
Parliament go. We think it is the fairest thing to do. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Iain Lees-Galloway—5 minutes.
2306 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: This is my first
opportunity to speak on the Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament
Remuneration) Amendment Bill. I have not been following the debate this afternoon, so
I apologise if I traverse—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: What?

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: I know. It is a shock. I apolo gise if I traverse material
that has been traversed by other members previously. Let us be honest about why it is
that we find ourselves debating this legislation. It is because the independent
Remuneration Authority, in determining the salary increases th at MPs should receive,
determined a level that it believed was fair but was significantly out of kilter with what
ordinary New Zealanders have received in terms of pay rises over the last 6 years or so.
We have heard on a number of occasions that the Prime  Minister has said that in his
opinion MPs’ pay does not need to rise as much as it has done, and that people would
feel aggrieved about the pay increases that MPs get, but that is in the context, I say to
the Prime Minister, of ordinary working New Zealan ders not getting ahead under his
Government. I appreciate that the Greens have offered a Supplementary Order Paper
linking MPs’ pay to median wages, because median wages have barely moved under
this Government, certainly in real terms. Most people who are on the median wage
actually in real terms find themselves worse off today than they did 6 years ago.
It is interesting that the Government often talks about “average” wages, which are
pulled up by those at the very top getting proportionately very large pay increases whilst
those who are in the middle and on lower incomes are not really getting pay increases
that allow them to get ahead. That is why I think this Government so studiously avoids
talking about the median wage, but if it did and if it actually  talked about what ordinary
people who are on this middle income are getting, then the story would not be nearly as
rosy as it makes it out to be.
We agree with, and we will vote for, legislation that perhaps tries to pare back the
increases to our salari es to make them align more closely with what ordinary working
people get, but we really just do not think the process around this has been all that
clever. First of all, as we said, the Prime Minister has been talking about this for years
and years and years, and yet suddenly he felt the need to act. I think the suddenly came
along after some polling a couple of weekends ago. The focus groups probably told the
Prime Minister that he needed to act and he needed to act fast. And this is a Prime
Minister who is in need of some good news. Let us be honest. It has been a pretty rough
start to the year. The Prime Minister was in need of something to demonstrate that he
was in touch with the voters, and this one suddenly popped out of the box. It was going
to be de bated last week, but after it was tabled it was discovered that there were a few
flaws. The Government went back to the drawing board and it has come back to this this
week—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: What were the flaws?

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: Ruth Dyson asks what the flaws were. It is hard to
know even where to begin, but I think the fundamental flaw was possibly that we could
have ended up with a greater pay rise, as a result of the legislation, than we originally
were. There were problems with it, clearly. That is what happens when legislation is
drafted after a focus group on a Sunday afternoon and tabled at the beginning of the
week and then the intention is to put it through under urgency. So now we are back here
this week, hope fully with an improvement to the legislation. We will vote for this
because we think this is, hopefully, going to move things in the right direction, but we
suspect that we will be back in the future. If we do have to come back in the future, we
hope that we do this with an appropriate process that actually gives the full machinery
of government and all the officials the opportunity to have input into the drafting of the
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2307
legislation, and that it gives the public the opportunity to offer their thoughts so that we
can actually build a piece of legislation like we do normally. This is why we have the
process we have, so that we can build good, robust, long -lasting legislation that is
actually fit for purpose and does the job it is meant to do.
We are concerned that we are likely to find ourselves having to come back and
address this issue again in the future. We also have concerns —I know that others have
traversed this—around the fact that this links MPs’ pay to the public sector. The public
sector is actually the group of workers whose pay MPs have the most influence over. I
can see that the Assistant Speaker is indicating that I am coming close to time, so I will
take my seat, but I look forward to the Committee stage.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: You will take your seat, yes.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak on
the second rea ding of the Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament
Remuneration) Amendment Bill. As we have heard, the Minister has addressed various
issues raised by the Opposition. The main issue is that this issue cannot be addressed
without changing the legisla tion. The sole criterion that will determine a member of
Parliament’s pay increase has been debated, and the sole criterion in the bill is the right
one, which I will address later on.
The Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendm ent
Bill is to amend the Remuneration Authority Act 1977 to require the Remuneration
Authority to solely consider public sector wage movements when determining salary
increases for members of Parliament.
I am taking a short call to say that I am fully sup portive of this bill. This bill is about
fairness. This bill actually helps the Remuneration Authority so that the salaries of
members of Parliament, assessed under section 16(2) of the Members of Parliament
(Remuneration and Services) Act 2013, can move up in line with those in the public
sector. This bill sets the frequency of these adjustments. It also clarifies for the
Remuneration Authority if there is no movement in the average earnings in the public
sector.
There has been criticism from other parties of rushing this through. This bill has been
thoroughly thought through. It is time we address this issue, and not just talk about it.
The criticism from members of the public normally is that the pay increases of members
of Parliament are higher than those in the public sector. This bill is to address that issue.
As we know, this bill is going through all stages today under urgency. This is because
there is no justification seen in the Remuneration Authority’s determination of an
approximately 3.5 percent increase in the salaries of members of Parliament.
There were some comments from the Opposition about some positions in the public
sector and even the private sector being very highly paid. Those salaries are decided by
the market. Why would people  work in a country if they are not rewarded for the value
they add to the organisation? We need to be able to recruit and retain good people, but
this bill is not about their salary; this bill is about addressing the salary increases of
members of Parliament only.
The Government must ensure that people are listened to and are treated fairly, and
that is what this bill is about. We must lead by example, and that is why I support this
bill. I look forward to contributing more on later stages. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: Once again, at peak listening time, I
get the opportunity to take a call in this second reading of the Remuneration Authority
(Members of Parliament Remuner ation) Amendment Bill. I just have to acknowledge
the member who has just resumed her seat and say that that was a courageous attempt to
defend what has been a series of amazing errors on behalf of the Government. We were
told on Monday last week by the Le ader of the House: “There will be urgency
2308 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015
tomorrow to pass the Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament Remuneration)
Amendment Bill.” So we were all prepared. There was no sign of the bill. Actually,
there was no sign of the Leader of the House eithe r, but that is not always a bad thing.
Then we were told on Tuesday that the plans had changed and there would now be
urgency on Wednesday to correct the MPs’ pay issue. Wednesday came and went. We
were then told it was going to be Thursday. So in a 3- day sitting week we were told that
all 3 days would be the day for urgency, and then on Thursday we were told it would be
this week.
We received yesterday —or perhaps even earlier today; yesterday I think—version
7.3 of the Supplementary Order Paper that has now been incorporated into the bill. This
is not a well- considered, well -thought-through piece of legislation. The original draft
risked parliamentarians—

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: I’m hurt.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: I do not hold responsible the Minister who is braving it and
fronting it in the House. He may not have had the opportunity to read the latest version.
I am not sure whether it has been run past him, actually. But take the chance to, before
the third reading. It would be worth it. It would be worth it from our point of view to
have this bill, which is designed to correct the decision of the Remuneration
Authority—and I say “correct” in the broadest terms, because it has now become a
political exercise —to make sure that M Ps do not get a huge pay rise when, clearly,
other people deserve it much more. That is the point of this legislation.
The original legislation the Government was going to bring in several times last
week ran the risk of increasing the pay of members of P arliament even further than the
Remuneration Authority had proposed.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: Hon RUTH DYSON
items.text: As I was saying prior to the dinner adjournment, it is a good
opportunity during the second reading of the Remuneration Authority (Members of
Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill to compare the actions that are proposed in
this legislation with the portrayal by the Government of why it is taking this action
under urgency and, actually, what is happening in the rest of the world.
I certainly support this legislation, and all Labour members will be voting for it, but I
have to say that it is a bit of a mess. We had on three occasions last week, actually four
counting Monday, the Leader of the House saying that this  legislation would be
introduced under urgency the next day. The Minister Gerry Brownlee, Leader of the
House, said that to us on Monday. Tuesday came and went. It did not happen. On
Tuesday he said it would be introduced on Wednesday. Wednesday came and w ent—no
legislation. On Wednesday he said it would be Thursday. Thursday came and went.
Members returned home after the House rose—still no legislation.
Then today we have the legislation, with version 7.3 of the Supplementary Order
Paper. This has gone through a lot of changes. Now we are going through all stages
under urgency. The Supplementary Order Paper has now been incorporated into the bill.
It is another structural change to the legislation that we are considering, rather than
having that as a Suppl ementary Order Paper, and none of the opportunities of the usual
consideration of a select committee.
Even though it has taken the Government 6 years to decide that the process of the
Remuneration Authority for setting MPs’ wages is not what it likes —it has been in
power for 6 long years —now we get under urgency, through all stages, a bill that has
clearly been problematic. The bill that was going to be introduced last week could not
be introduced, for a very good reason. The errors in it were detected at the last minute—
I do not know who detected them. It was possibly the Hon Christopher Finlayson. He
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2309
seems to be one who actually reads legislation; he is the only one whom I have noticed,
actually, out of the entire Cabinet. Somebody picked up the fact tha t the proposed
legislation ran the risk of actually increasing the salaries of members of Parliament by
more than the Remuneration Authority had suggested, and clearly that was not a runner.
Although we support this legislation I have to say that the Gove rnment portraying
itself as being fairer is a total nonsense. I do not think it is good practice to put in rushed
legislation, through all stages under urgency, if you are serious about fixing a problem.
It certainly could have been done some time ago. We knew that this issue was going to
come up. Again, prior to Christmas last year there could have been some proper cross -
party talks about an alternative mechanism for fixing the salaries of members of
Parliament that could be open and transparent, and that the public could have some
confidence in.
At the same time as this legislation is going through and the Government is saying:
“We are doing this because we want to be fair.”, the Prime Minister and the Minister of
Finance are announcing, via the media, to the public servants of New Zealand that they
are going to have their wage increase, promised by the Prime Minister and the Minister
of Finance during the 2014 election campaign, evaporate. Suddenly that promise, like
many of National’s promises, is worth absolutely nothing. Actually the National Party
campaigned on a promise of a good increase in the wages of public servants, and now it
is saying: “No, we cannot afford it.” I guess it wants to put some of that money into its
made-up surplus as well.
The Government has increased the minimum wage by a measly 50c an hour —50c an
hour—for the lowest -paid workers in New Zealand, and it is trying to portray itself as
fair and considerate. Well, it is obviously a nonsense. The Government is ripping off
New Zealand  workers and New Zealand businesses to the tune of —not a little bit—
$350 million a year, the equivalent of 700 jobs, that New Zealand workers and
employers are paying in overcharged ACC levies. They do not need to be charged that
much. They are paying too much in their ACC levies, and that money is being taken out
of ACC and put into a surplus. We have not seen that sort of behaviour since the Rt Hon

items.speaker: Robert Muldoon. This legislation is being portrayed as
items.text: “We want to be fair. We want to
make sure that MPs d o not get huge salary increases, while we are giving tuppence -
ha’penny to the people on the minimum wage.” But the truth is that is exactly what this
Government is doing.
This has been quite a hashed process, as I indicated. Last week we had several
indications from the Leader of the House about this legislation being introduced under
urgency, and it has come in only today. We did have over seven versions of the
Supplementary Order Paper, none of which made sense. There has not been any public
debate on wh at should be the core principles if the Remuneration Authority regime is
going to be changed. In my view they are that the setting of any salaries for members of
Parliament should not be made by members of Parliament; they should be independent,
it should be publicly transparent and accountable, and it should have fair considerations.
Part of that should be the consideration of what other people in our society are getting in
terms of their wage remuneration.
I remember in the 2009 Budget, the first Budget that this National- led Government
brought in, there were massive tax cuts for the wealthiest people in New Zealand and at
the same time there were cuts to home -care services for older New Zealanders. There
was also nothing to help the wages of the people on the lowest income, the minimum
wage workers, in New Zealand. Bill English said during that debate in Parliament that if
people in New Zealand wanted to earn more money, they should work harder. That is
what he said in this House —if people wanted to earn more money, they should work
harder.
2310 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015
I know that all members of Parliament work hard and come into this House to do
better for their country. It is the highest form of public service, but it is by no means the
only form of public service. So we should not  get paid more than we are worth. Public
servants in New Zealand should get paid what they are worth and they are not, and
people on the minimum wage deserve to have their contribution valued more. Thank
you.
A party vote  was called for on the question, That the Remuneration Authority
(Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
Ayes 106
New Zealand National 59; New Zealand Labour 32; New Zealand First 11; Māori
Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 14

Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and

items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is
