I want to finish by addressing, with your tolerance, Mr Chairman, a comment made
by the Minister in the chair himself: “We all want a high -wage economy.” Well, zero -
hour contracts do not give you that, manipulating employment statistics for people who
work only 1 hour a week do not give you that, and driving down wages by employing
foreign students and misusing and abusing foreign labour do not give you that, Minister.

items.speaker: METIRIA T UREI
items.text: I just wanted to address the other two
Supplementary Order Papers in my name, which I have not talked about yet, but also
just to note for the public two things. First, the Minister has confirmed that this bill will
not constrain MPs’ pay. What it does is it locks in increases. It will not constrain MPs’
pay. MPs’ pay will continue to grow at a percentage level and therefore increase the gap
between MPs and the lower -paid workers in this country. That is what this change will
do. It is one of the reasons why we are not supporting this bill.
The second thing I would say is that the Minister went on at length in the Committee
stage about constraining Public Service pay, constraining Government spending, which
clearly demonstrates the p urpose of this bill. This bill is not designed to meet the
public’s concerns about MPs’ pay increases; it is designed to have a mechanism to
justify keeping Public Service pay low. That was clear in the reasoning. The Minister
has spent more time talking a bout this as a mechanism to keep Public Service pay low
than about the public concern around MPs’ pay increases, which clearly shows the
purpose of this bill.
I have two Supplementary Order Papers, still. I have described one; I have another
one, Supplementary Order Paper 59, which uses a different mechanism in terms of the
Public Service. What this one does is it uses the labour cost index from the labour
market statistics. This Supplementary Order Paper is an alternative to the first one. It
would mean t hat since 2007 MPs’ pay, instead of going up by $30,000, which it does
under the current regime, would have gone up by only $14,000. So we would have had
half the pay increases over the last few years than we do have under the current
situation. It is a me ans to constrain MPs’ pay and is a much better measure for Public
Service pay than the quarterly employment survey, because this bill bases the change in
salary and wage rates for the Public Service, but it is a better measure.
The labour market statistic s are a much truer measure of the actual rate of increase
than the quarterly employment survey because they measure what people are actually
being paid by employers. This would mean it is a much fairer approach to using the
Public Service as some kind of m easure. It does mean there would have been a
significant decrease in MPs’ pay over the last 6 years, so it is a genuine constraint. The
quarterly employment survey can be used but it is a very crude measure. What it does in
the Government’s bill is it essentially maintains the status quo and locks in increases.
Employers ask Statistics New Zealand about information on pay rates and they ask
about the labour cost index. It is a truer measure of public sector pay. The State Services
Commission uses the labour cost index. Its Human Resource Capability Survey of
Public Service departments uses the labour cost index. Even the State Services
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2329
Commission thinks it is a better measure for looking at pay rates across the public
sector.
Importantly, we have also linked this to the changes in salary and wages for the
Public Service as opposed to the public sector. The public sector is not an exact group to
use for something this important. It is a much wider pool and includes higher wage
movements in health, education, and local government. The Public Service is narrower
and it puts MPs in a much closer position to public servants as they are more commonly
understood, so it is a better measure. If the intention of the parties is to have a measure
that is related to the Public Service, then our Supplementary Order Paper 59 is a much
better, clearer measure and it actually will constrain MPs’ pay increases.
Our third Supplementary Order Paper, which my colleague James Shaw has also
touched on, is the one that essentially removes everything in the bill except for the bit
that revokes the current determination. So this Supplementary Order Paper 58, if it went
through, would mean that the current determination of the Remuneration Authority to
increase MPs’ pay would be stoppe d. It would mean that this new determination would
not proceed, so MPs would not get their pay rise. But it would also mean that there is no
additional measure, so the current pay and conditions that MPs are working under
would remain. Doing that would give us time to look at this bill through a select
committee process and to have an opportunity for MPs and parties to look at each
other’s alternatives.
I do accept that for other parties that have looked at our Supplementary Order Papers,
I understand their concern that they simply have not had time to assess them properly
because there has not been time as part of the bill because we are in urgency. So it
would mean that there would be alternatives other than the Greens’. The Māori Party,
New Zealand First, the Labour Party, ACT —I do not know whether it is supporting the
bill; I would be very surprised about that, but ACT may have ideas about how to
constrain MPs’ pay. All of those ideas would be able to be put on the table and
presented to the public. The public would have a chance to investigate and interrogate
those ideas and to come to us and tell us what kinds of conditions, what criteria, and
what constraints they would like to see, and we would be able to come up with an
enduring solution.
So there is an option on the table tonight for political parties to stop the current pay
increase—that is Supplementary Order Paper 58 —and then for us to step back a bit,
have another look at the Minister’s bill, take it through a select committee process
properly, and have a fuller investigation as to what is the right measure, because, I
agree, there is no doubt that there are going to be mistakes in this and we are going to
have to come back. And, as can happen, the mistake could be a significant
embarrassment to the Government. It is the kind of thing where you could see where
maybe there will be significant pay increases instead, which is not the Government’s
intention, and it will have to come back to us and ask us to support fixing its mistake.
Frankly, tha t would be extremely difficult to tolerate and stomach, because the
Government has been well warned—the Minister has been well warned —that a mistake
is likely and that there were alternatives on the table to prevent that from happening. So
I would urge mem bers to vote in favour of the preferred option, which is tying MPs’
pay to the nominal median wage.
The second option is tying it to the labour cost index, which is a Public Service
measure but a more appropriate, tighter Public Service measure. And, thir d, if you do
not like either of those measures, then at least vote for the third Supplementary Order
Paper to stop the current pay increase, so that we can go away and have a good and
decent look at this legislation.
2330 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015
The fact is, the Government has got the numbers. The Government has got the
numbers to pass whatever legislation it chooses —at least for the moment; that is true —
so there is no need for urgency. The Minister has made no argument at all for urgency.
He has not said a single thing about why it a ll has to be done tonight while the rest of
the country is watching The Bachelor New Zealand and is very distracted, I understand.
There is no justification for doing this in urgency, and he has made none because there
is none. So it really is shocking tha t something so serious could be treated so trivially,
but given his own argument that the core reason for this bill is actually to constrain
Public Service pay, then I guess we cannot be surprised. It is a shame that National
would treat both the Remunerat ion Authority and the New Zealand public, and
particularly the Public Service, in such a shabby way. Thank you.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: I just wanted to rise and take a call
on this at this stage because I wanted to assure the New Zealand public who are
watching—because this is far more riveting than The Bachelor New Zealand—that in
fact we have considered Supplementary Order Papers 57, 58, and 59 that the Green
Party has put forward, and discussed them in the length of time that we have been given
to discuss them at length, and come up with what we think are our answers to this. The
Greens have suggested in Supplementary Order Paper 57 that the median wage be the
determining factor for whether we go up or go down. If the median wage goes up $100
then our MPs’ wages go up $100. Essentially the idea is not a bad one, but there is just
not the time in the shortened period that we have had to look at it to put enough detail
around that, and what about this, what about that, and what other factors might then
impact on that.
In a different Supplementary Order Paper they have suggested attaching MPs’ wages
to the two indexes, the quarterly employment survey and the labour cost index. The
quarterly employment survey is based on actual, real people. In fact, if we look at it
consistently, we also have the paid parental funding and the superannuation determined
by the quarterly employment survey, and it is about actual people. We actually thi nk
that that is OK. The labour cost index is about wage inflation and it is done on a
statistical, theoretical basis, so we are happy to support the Supplementary Order Paper,
which talks about the quarterly employment survey. This is because I am an exper t in
these fields and I have taken all the due consideration of the time given to us to consider
this. We have rung people. We have gone out to our constituents. We have discussed it.
We have tried to do what we need to do to ensure that we are supporting something that
we can, hand on heart, say that we think this is what we should support given the
circumstances that we are in.
According to the Remuneration Authority, apparently the Remuneration Authority
could not use its discretion because of a piece of legislation that talked about equality. If
we talked about setting our wages at the same level as people who work in a similar
area across the public and private sectors, then MPs’ wages would go up, and that is
what it determined. There was no appetite for that and that is why we are here having
this conversation under urgency. The whole country stood up and said: “Please do not
do this. That is ridiculous.” The reason they did it is because we do not give the same
urgency to low incomes, the minimum wag e, and the levels of benefit, which need to
have some urgency applied to them. That is why our people are living in poverty, and
we need to adjust that.
I want to assure the public that we have considered the Supplementary Order Papers
that the Greens hav e put forward. I want to thank the Greens for putting them forward
because at least they have given us some options to look at. In this stage we think that
we are happy with the legislation that has been put forward as it stands given the short
period of t ime. We would have liked some more time. We would have liked the
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2331
opportunity for the public to have submissions around this. Given the circumstances, we
are happy to support it. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDO N
items.text: I just wanted to briefly make a couple of further
points, firstly about the commencement, which of course is the day after a procedural
assent, etc., but in fact this is retrospective legislation. The effect of this legislation is to
take us back to a day or a week before the Remuneration Authority fulfilled its mandate
to come up with a proposal about an increase or a change in MPs’ salaries, and to
pretend that never happened.
We generally are very suspicious of retrospective legislation. I am  not blind to the
fact that our third -choice Supplementary Order Paper —I think— also suggests a
retrospective move, to basically overturn the decision that was made. But not then to
endeavour in the course of a week to cobble together in haste an inadequate  substitute
for that decision- making process, which, flawed as it may be —and we do agree
absolutely that is has been flawed for a very long time. We wonder why the
Government has not taken steps, if it is genuinely concerned that that process of setting
remuneration is flawed. Why has it waited until this moment to shove through a bill in
the course of a few hours on a Tuesday afternoon? I do think that that is a point that we
have yet to hear an answer from the Minister about. What is the basis of the rati onale or
the excuse for urgency?
The other point I would like to comment on, again, is that the bill talks about a 12-
month cycle. If we had the luxury of a proper parliamentary process, if we could take
advice from elsewhere and listen to submissions, we  might hear an argument —and it
has been put before —that ought we not, perhaps, put this on a 36- month cycle rather
than a 12- month cycle, so that MPs come into this House at each election knowing
roughly what their income, their package of benefits, and so on is going to be for the
next 3 years? I would argue that might take some of the heat out of the public objection.
At least it would be 3 -yearly rather than an annual circus. I would suggest that if we do
benchmark MPs’ salary movements to some average, then you have got a 3- year
average rather than a 12 -month one, which I think would make it more robust,
potentially more reliable, and longer lasting.
Again, these are symptoms of something that has been cobbled together in great
haste without adequate thought, and without drawing on the undoubted expertise that is
available in the communities of interest—be they specialised or simply the members of
the public who might want to have a say. I wonder whether part of the Government’s
determination to have this done and dusted in a few hours on a Tuesday is because it is
unwilling to expose itself to the public, to public input, because undoubtedly a select
committee looking at some alternative proposition would take the opportunity to have a
crack at MPs. You would hear a lot of opinion, a lot of rhetoric undoubtedly, and that is
fair comment. Maybe we ought to simply expose ourselves to that, have a proper
process, and think about things like whether we should look at a 3-year rather than a 12-
month cycle, and whether we ought not underline the public outcry about MP
remuneration. Should we not stop and think to ourselves: “Why is it that the public
objects so strongly to MPs getting paid a bit more?”
Maybe it is something to do with the behaviour that is rout inely displayed in this
House, not least of all at question time —the yelling, the shouting, the behaviour that
ought not be accepted in a third- form English class in any college on a given afternoon.
Perhaps we need to look a bit more closely at ourselves, our own behaviours, and our
own practices for an explanation of why the public does get so very angry when they
see MPs apparently getting an increase in pay. I think—to channel our former colleague
Mr Robertson—that maybe we need to think again about a c ode of conduct for this
House. Maybe if the public saw us behaving in a way befitting members of this
2332 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015
Chamber more often and more routinely, maybe some of the heat would go out of this
debate and it would become more rational, more focused, and a little bi t more objective
than it currently is. Thank you.

Third Reading
Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and
Safety): I move, That the Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament
Remuneration) Amendment Bill be now read a third time . The bill is the Government’s
response to the most recent determination of the Remuneration Authority, which
provides for an increase in the remuneration received by MPs of 3.56 percent, effective
from 1 July 2014. The Government considers this increase to be disproportionate to the
salary movements in the wider public sector and unfair to taxpayers. The bill limits the
Remuneration Authority consideration to applying the wage growth in the public sector,
as measured by the quarterly employment survey, to MPs’ remuneration. The bill
provides a fair response to the disproportionate increase in MPs’ remuneration by
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2333
providing a measure that reflects the average growth in public sector wages. This
ensures that the taxpayer is not unfairly burdened by any unwarranted increases in
remuneration. In summation, the Government believes that these alignments will align
MPs’ remuneration with that of the wider public sector and will strike the right balance
between the interests of taxpayers and those whose remuneration is being assessed. I
commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: That was a slightly shorter contribution
from the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety, Michael Woodhouse, than I was
anticipating. I am happy to rise to do my final contribution in this debate on the
Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill. I
want to just first of all say that the mechanism that this House establishes for
determining how MPs’ pay s hould be set is a very important one constitutionally. It is
not good practice for Parliament itself to be voting on, debating, and setting, effectively,
what the taxpayer should pay us for doing this job. It is important that we put in place a
robust mechanism that removes those decisions from this House and places them with
an independent body that can make those decisions rigorously and independently.
I think the public of New Zealand would like to have that reassurance that in fact we
are not here feat hering our own nests and debating things that are going to be in our
own best interests and that there is someone independent making decisions about what a
fair rate of pay for members of Parliament should be. This is, in fact, an important issue.
No one here is arguing for a significant pay increase at the moment, but ensuring that
MPs receive a sufficient and appropriate level of remuneration is actually important for
the transparency and integrity of the democratic system of government. It is actually one
of the guards that we have against corruption. Making sure that MPs are appropriately
remunerated for the job that we do is one of the ways that the public of New Zealand
and the taxpayer can have the reassurance that we are working for them and not for
other people who are paying us and giving us money for the work that we do. The only
way that the public can have the assurance that that is what is happening is when those
decisions are made completely independently of this House and when there are robust
criteria for doing so.
It has been apparent for some time now that there were issues with the criteria that
the Remuneration Authority had in determining what MPs’ pay should be, and it is high
time that the House resolved those issues. This is not a good process for doing that. We
have had 5 years of concerns. We have had 5 years where the criteria could have been
properly and appropriately amended without the need to resort to urgency. It is,
therefore, unfortunate that we now find ourselves in this pos ition where if we do not
conclude this debate this week under urgency —through all of the bill’s stages —then
MPs will get the significant pay increases next week that we are here tonight trying to
stop from happening. That could have been avoided if this ha d been dealt with through
a much better, more rigorous, and proper process. Unfortunately, that has not happened,
and therefore urgency is the only way now to stop those pay rises going through and
being in MPs’ bank accounts next week.
We on the Labour P arty side have listened very carefully to the debate and we have
engaged with it in good faith, with the principle being that we wanted to stop those rises
going through and we wanted to make sure that the criteria are amended in a way that is
robust and that will provide an enduring and independent solution for how MPs’ pay is
set. That is the reason that we voted in favour of the legislation and in favour of
urgency, because without urgency, as I have said, there would have been no way to stop
those pay increases.
However, having listened to the debate, we did vote in favour of Supplementary
Order Paper 58 put forward by Metiria Turei, which would have resulted in the
2334 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015
legislation being passed now but stopping only those pay increases, and leaving for
another day the decision around what the new criteria should be, because we do not
think that this is a good process. We would rather that it went through a more rigorous
process, particularly, and this is a big issue for me because I would like to ensure that
the Remuneration Authority —the experts on this; the people who have to actually
implement it—is able to provide some scrutiny of the legislation that we are now
passing. It has not had the opportunity to do so and it will not have the opportunity to do
so. As a result we cannot be sure that the legislation that we are passing now is actually
going to do what it purports to do in the short term and in the long term. There is a
possibility that in the long term this will give us bigger pay increases than the  existing
criteria that we have, which we are now replacing. That is one of the reasons there needs
to be greater scrutiny of these matters —so that we can be sure that the bill does what it
is supposed to do. We do not have that because of the way this process has been rushed.
One of the concerning things that became very apparent during the debate is that this
debate is, in fact, only partly about MPs’ pay and that, actually, the wider agenda from
the Government is to suppress the pay overall across the w hole of the public sector,
including teachers, doctors, nurses, police, prison officers, and so on—we could go on
and on through all of the professions. It is very disappointing to hear members from the
National Party referring to those who work for the good of the public and who want pay
increases as union thugs. I think that is very disappointing. I think that after a long
period of time when their pay rises have not kept up with inflation—in fact, in real
terms their salaries have gone backwards —it is fa ir enough that they are asking for a
pay increase.
I heard Bill English claiming —I think it was either today or yesterday —that, in fact,
teachers, for example, have had pay rises above inflation. So I went and looked at the
top of the teacher salary scale.  These are the most experienced teachers, the longest -
serving—teachers, the ones who do not have any other management roles or whatever
and who are just simply at the top of the teacher salary scale. Here are the real numbers:
in 2009 they were paid $68,980 and as of last year they were paid $72,646. So let us be
clear. These are the most experienced teachers. That is a 5.3 percent pay increase. What
did inflation do during that time? It was 9.3 percent during that time. Actually, in real
terms, a teacher w ho has no management responsibilities and who is at the top of the
salary scale has gone backwards in the last 4 or 5 years under this National
Government, and yet Bill English is saying that they should not be getting any pay
increase at all. They have seen the real value of their incomes eroded during that time.
So the Government is up against the wall this year when a lot of these big public
sector collective agreements come up for negotiation because actually people have been
promised for 5 years by this Government —and maybe longer —that there will be jam
tomorrow, but jam never actually comes, and they are saying that they have had enough
of that. I think that is quite understandable. I think it is wrong that the Government uses
this debate on MPs’ pay to try to suppress the debate over wider pay issues within the
public sector. I do not think MPs should be getting significant pay increases of the
magnitude that were recently awarded, but I actually do think it is probably time to look
at some of those pay rates in the public sector because there has been a lot of belt
tightening.
Finally, I just want to make one last contribution in this debate, and that is around the
actual formula that this bill is now establishing, which links MP pay increases to the
average increases within the public sector. As I have raised during earlier parts of this
debate, that can create some unintended consequences because the overall average
increase in the public sector can be distorted by higher -than-average increases in
managerial salaries for those at the top of the salary scale and lower increases for those
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2335
who are on regular and low incomes. As a result, our pay will go up while the pay of the
people whom we are most interested in protecting —the people out there who are  not
getting pay increases—continues to go backwards. So this formula does not necessarily
deliver on the sentiment and the value proposition that the Government is putting
forward, which is one of the reasons why this rushed process is not acceptable. The
Labour Party has supported this bill going through simply because we had no choice. It
was the only way to stop those significant pay increases going through next week. It is
not good process. The Government could have, and should have, acted on this much,
much earlier.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity
to speak on the third reading of this bill. Can I just say there were some pertinent points
that Chris Hipkins, the previous speaker, made, and thank you for the support that he
and his colleagues have given to this bill. I think when we look at how the
Remuneration Authority determines its salary bands and settings, one of the things that
it does do is look at fair relativity with comparable positions, the need to be fair to both
individuals whose pay is being set and to taxpayers, the requirements of the job, the
need to recruit and retain competent individuals, and any prevailing adverse economic
conditions.
I guess, in many regards, the mystery of the magic of how all of this comes together
is now being faced with a different process, which I believe brings transparency. Every
year the salaries are set in accordance with this formula, so that we ar e not going to get
any big surprises and huge headlines. It is going to be predictable. It is going to be
something that the public sector across the board has already received the previous year.
I think, in many regards, people in our country will say thi s is a process that is going to
work and brings that degree of transparency, certainty, and, I would say, even
equivalency through this process. I am very happy, in the final reading of this bill, to
commend it to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY

items.speaker: ANDREW BAYLY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise to lend my support
to this Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendment
Bill of 2015. This bill is all about MPs showing leadership. We, as MPs, need to
demonstrate restraint. It is only appropriate that this bi ll makes these changes. The
Prime Minister foreshadowed some of his concern and the outcomes are just. Aligning
our pay to the public sector is a good way to go. It is fair, it is equitable, and it is
reasonable. I commend the bill to the House. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: The Green Party will continue to oppose
this legislation. I want to thank Labour and New Zealand First for supporting
Supplementary Order Paper 58—the one to restrict MPs’ pay rises so that it would have
given us a chance to deal with the substantive legi slation in a more timely and
democratic manner. I really do appreciate that support. I also understand how difficult it
is to have to deal with Supplementary Order Papers at such short notice for parties, so
thank you for your consideration.
We are opposing this legislation because it does not do what the Government says it
wants it to do. It is actually designed for an entirely different purpose. The purpose of
the legislation, as we have seen described by the Minister in his contributions during the
Committee stage, is to constrain public sector pay. That became very, very obvious
from the Minister’s statements. He talked about “profligate public spending” —is that
right? There were comments from the National Party about “union thugs”. I think both
of thos e comments, just in such a short debate on what should otherwise have been
quite a tight conversation about MPs’ pay increases, just go to show that there is no
2336 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015
intention by National to constrain MPs’ pay. It is simply using the political opportunity
of this supposedly huge public outrage to attack ordinary workers —people like teachers
and nurses, people who are involved in the Public Service, people who dedicate their
lives to helping New Zealanders get through the various circumstances that they have to
get through. National is clearly intent on attacking them. It follows on from other
legislation that National has put forward that has taken out the tea breaks, for example,
for New Zealand workers, and that has continued the plan of National since it took
Government to erode the conditions of workers in the private sector and, increasingly,
in the public sector. This legislation has been used to do exactly that.
New Zealanders should rightly feel that they have been manipulated by National
through the use of this bill and that their concerns about MPs’ pay rises have been
trodden on by National with this bill because this bill does not constrain MPs’ pay, but
is being used to attack their own people. When we are talking about New Zealanders in
a context lik e this, we are talking about people who are in the Public Service or have
dedicated their lives in some form to the public sector. We are talking about family
members of people who work in the Public Service. We are not that far removed from
each other in this country. We are a little, tiny country, and we are very connected to
each other. There is no real “us” and “them”, and so when Government uses legislation
and manipulates legitimate public concern for nefarious political purpose —that is,
keeping pay l ow for workers —every MP in this House should be seriously concerned
and prepared to tell the New Zealand public what is being done to them by this
Government.
Our initial assessment of this legislation was that it failed to do the job that it was
supposed to do. Our committed opposition to this bill continues and is strengthened
because it is so clear that this was a manipulative exercise by the Prime Minister, the
Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety, and the National Government, and we
will have no part of it. The Green Party is opposed to this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora Mr Assistant Speaker. I
rise for the final contribution of New Zealand First on the bill, and I pick up on the
comments made by Metiria Turei. It is unfortunate that it appears the Government has
taken an opportunity to actually step on the workers of New Zealand. New Zealand First
is very disappointed that Supplementary Order Paper 58, which the Green Party put up,
and which would have split off and therefore stopped the 3.5 percent increase for MPs
here tonight —but that Supplementary Order Paper would have sent the conversation
about the Remuneration Authority’s set of criteria by which it sets the pay of members
of Parliament through a much longer process. It would have sent that back and into
another bill that would have gone through the select committee process, which the New
Zealand public would have had the opportunity to speak about.
If the purpose here today is to say to the New Zealand public that we, the members
of Parliament, understand that times are tough—and they are tougher for some than they
are for others —and if the purpose of this moment in time is to say that we understand
that, that could have been done by a single piece of legislation that said: “We will not
accept that.” It was not a requirement for us to actually come up with another formula
here tonight. New Zealand First agrees with the Labour Party —we are concerned about
the formula. The fact that it was version seven by the time we got to 10.30 today, with
people manipulating algebra here, there, and everywhere, gives nobod y any confidence
that this is right. Not a single one of us —and, actually, not a single backbencher —
understands that equation, I guarantee it.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: That’s not right.
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2337

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Guarantee it —you might not be sitting on the backbench
tonight, Mr Foster -Bell, but I will guarantee that the ones who are do not understand
that equation. But that is not the point.
It is really unfortunate that the conversation ended up going down to comments like
“union thugs”. It is very, very unfortunate. That was not the purpose that we were all
here for tonight. It was unnecessary. This was supposed to be about us making sure that
the New Zealand public —and Mr Bayly keeps saying it —saw leadership from us. It is
very unfortunate that, as it would appear through the statements made by the Minister
for Workplace Relations and Safety and through other members, this is actually not
about us. This is about controlling New Zealanders as they enter into what are supposed
to be negotia tions. It is a great shame that that is where this Parliament has come to —
that we are prepared to legislate now to stop free and frank and honest negotiations
between workers and ourselves. It is an indictment upon this Parliament.
The other thing that we  do need to be careful of —and New Zealand First, again,
agrees with the contribution by Mr Hipkins; it has been particularly enlightening, Mr
Hipkins’ contribution, and it has been very worthwhile listening to—is around the word
“corruption”. I know it is hard sometimes, but sometimes the truth has to be said, and in
this moment, with this contribution, Mr Hipkins has been enlightening. It is around the
word “corruption”, and it is quite a serious thing, to be frank. It is around the word
“corruption”. There was a time in this Parliament when the only people who could come
to it were rich, white men who had independent means. They were the only people who
could come here. The only reason we have the diversity we have today is that we have a
system that supports a variety of representation. We must make sure that we, the
Parliament, do not turn this thing so far back that we end up with rich, white men as
representatives for us all, because we know how badly that works.
New Zealand First is disappointed. We w ill support this bill. We will support it
because we must stop the 3.5 percent pay rise for ourselves when we cannot share it
across our nation with other people. That is true. But we also would reiterate, again, that
we would have preferred the criteria t o be set with the public, not by us on the public,
because at the end of the day they pay us, and they should have had a voice in that
algebraic equation. Kia ora.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: JAMES SHAW
items.text: I would like to start by thanking the public servants who
helped to draft the legislation and who were in here later tonight, after hours, t o help
guide it through the House. It must have been hard for them to hear the Minister say that
one of the motivations for this bill was to hold down their wages in the future.
I think that there are a number of flaws with this bill. The Government’s moti vation
for tying MPs’ remuneration to that of the public sector, specifically, is one of them. In
saying to public servants and teachers and firefighters and doctors and nurses and so on
that we are going to tell members of Parliament that they should be a fraid of the public
backlash on their own pay in order to hold down your pay is, I think, absolutely
outrageous, and it is one of the reasons why we are opposed to this bill.
It is poor -quality legislation —we can see that. We have no idea what the actual
impact of this will be. There was no regulatory impact statement. We brought numbers
to this House analysing what we knew of the bill last week. We brought numbers to the
House that showed what the changes would have been under both of our Supplementary
Order Papers, but the Minister did not do that. We have actually not been shown by the
Government what the actual impact of this legislation would be. So we are about to pass
a bill and we do not actually know what it is and, as a number of people have said, most
people in this House who are voting for it do not know what the algebraic equation in
the bill actually means—what it says. It is a shocking piece of lawmaking.
2338 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015
That is, in large part, because it is being passed under urgency, and I would like to
say that the National Government has had 6 long years to do something about what is
now considered a burning issue. Six long years —long years —in which it has done
absolutely nothing until the last 10 days, when all of a sudden it was so important, it
was so important, that we had to use urgency as if this was some kind of national
emergency. It is not a national emergency; it is an emergency for National. This is not
worthy of an abuse of this process. The Minister has provided no case for this bill to
come through under urgency. We could have put this through under a normal legislative
programme. We could have had select committee stages, we could have heard the
evidence, we could have heard from the public, we could have weighed the options, and
we would hav e had a much higher -quality bill, where people actually understood what
the impact was going to be when they voted for it. They would have actually understood
that, but tonight, instead, we are going to vote on a bill, it is going to pass, and we have
no idea what it is actually going to do, except in some kind of theory.
I would like to thank Labour and New Zealand First, in particular, and I would also
like to thank the Māori Party for its gracious words about the Supplementary Order
Papers that we put f orward in Metiria Turei’s name. We know that because this is such
a poor-quality piece of legislation —a number of MPs have said this —we will be back
in the House talking about this legislation before too long, because we know that it is
busted. So we will be fixing it, and we will be calling on those who supported us tonight
on those Supplementary Order Papers for their support to fix the legislation and to tie
MP remuneration to the New Zealand median wage, which would tie MPs’ economic
interests to those of all New Zealanders. If we were to do that, our pay would rise and
fall with the pay of the country as a whole.
So we have made that case, we appreciate that it has been listened to by both sides of
the House, and we have done everything that we can on this one. We will continue to
hold that flame alive. We will not be voting for this bill, although some people have
said that this is some kind of improvement on the status quo. But we will not be voting
for something that is such an appalling abuse of process and such a poor -quality piece
of legislation. It is better to retain the status quo, and to allow that to happen, than it is
to put through such a shoddy piece of legislation. We will be looking forward to the
next time —and I cannot imagine it will be  too long —that we have to address this.
Thank you.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: Although the Māori Party
congratulates the Prime Minister on moving at lightning speed to address the obvious
anomalies, and although we are about making change —and this is one that we
support—while we are at it, let us be bold. Let us have the courage to take a fresh look
at the bigger picture of income inequality. I am reminded of the wisdom of Dr Martin

items.speaker: Luther King Jnr
items.text: “The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of
comfort and convenience, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy.”
The challenge and controversy has to be in tackling head -on the widening income
inequality and, in particular, to understand the financial material hardship of whānau
Māori.
A recent study by Lisa Marriott and Dalice Sim revealed that, although New Zealand
has had some success in reducing inequalities, the gaps in inequality among the
majority of the indicators investigated in this study show worsening outcomes for Māori
and Pacific people. A total of 21 indicators were investigated, including health,
knowledge, skills, employment, standards of living, cultural identity, and social
connectedness. Of those 21, 12 indicators —57 percent —reported increasing gaps
between Māori and non-Māori over the last decade.
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2339
So this is where we come to whānau ora. One of the six outcomes that we might
expect to see whānau succeeding in under favourable condit ions is wealth creation, so
we want to add that concept into the discussion. How is it fair that on one hand we can
give out 50c, and on the other hand we still will see an increase of about $5,000 and
more under this piece of legislation? Let us not just settle ourselves into being satisfied
with that new public sector index while that means that MPs’ salaries will still increase
in line with average public sector salaries, because all that those parallel increases will
do is sustain and retain the existing inequalities of remuneration.
We all know that inequality has a long- term effect. Income inequality experienced
early in life leads to reduced social mobility later in life. I understand that we are
running out of time. I know that we want to get this t hrough and we have come here
under urgency, but I want to make these points. We could investigate having a living
wage. The Māori Party thinks it should be $18.80. We currently have a minimum wage
that is set at a level of poverty. We are paying people to be impoverished, and that needs
to change. We should add urgency to that. Let us address income inequality in this
country. I like the fact that we are doing something about this and we are taking it
seriously, but there is so much more that we need to take seriously in regard to income.

items.speaker: I will finish with this
items.text: successive parliaments have created abject failure in
addressing income inequality in a meaningful way. Labour or National, Māori Party or
the Greens —whatever ideas have come up through members’ or  Government bills,
through select committees or question time, the point is we still have not fixed the
widening gaps. We are pleased that we have moved quickly and clearly to fix the issues
around the remuneration of MPs, but if we can move that rapidly f or this issue, why not
apply the same rigour to looking at the issue of income inequality and addressing the
enduring circumstances associated with whānau poverty in a sustainable, effective, and
mana-enhancing way? Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: I support the Remuneration Authority
(Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill and commend the bill to the
House. Thank you.
A party vote  was called for o n the question, That the Remuneration Authority
(Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill be now read a third time.
Ayes 106
New Zealand National 59; New Zealand Labour 32; New Zealand First 11; Māori
Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 14
Green Party 14.
Bill read a third time.

TUESDAY, 17 MARCH 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
MOTIONS 
Cyclone Pam—Expression of Support for Vanuatu and Other Pacific Countries 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : I seek leave to move a motion without 
notice in relation to Cyclone Pam. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is none. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I move, That the House express its support for the people and 
Government of Vanuatu and other Pacific neighbours affected by Cyclone Pam . Over 
the weekend, Cyclone Pam cut a path through the Pacific, resulting in reports of damage 
from Fiji, Tuvalu, Kiribati, and the Solomon Islands. However, the most severely 
affected country is Vanuatu. When tropical Cyclone Pam hit Vanuatu, it was a category 
5 cyclo ne with winds gusting up to 320 kilometres per hour. In the Efate province, 
where Vanuatu’s capital, Port Vila, is located, 90 percent of structures have been 
destroyed or damaged in some way. Thousands have been left homeless, and sadly there 
are now reports of 24 confirmed fatalities. The most concerning thing is that reports of 
damage are still to come in from the outlying islands and remote provinces. Cyclone 
Pam is already the worst disaster in Vanuatu’s recent history, and as we get a better 
picture of the damage outside Port Vila, we cannot rule out the scale of this catastrophe 
increasing dramatically. The thoughts of all New Zealanders are with the people of 
Vanuatu at this difficult time, and we want our neighbours in the Pacific to know that 
they do not face this disaster alone.  
As soon as we were able to on Saturday we launched a Royal New Zealand Air 
Force P3 Orion to conduct damage assessment flights over Tuvalu, the first nation in 
Cyclone Pam’s path. As the first reports of damage came in, we announced an initial $1 
million contribution in funding to respond to specific requests for assistance in Vanuatu, 
Fiji, Tuvalu, and the Solomon Islands and for NGOs in Vanuatu and the Solomon 
Islands to replenish relief supplies. We also sent a Royal New  Zealand Air Force C130 
to Vanuatu carrying 8 tonnes of relief supplies and emergency personnel. There have 
now been two further relief flights to Vanuatu and we have upped our funding 
contribution to $2.5 million. Additional aid flights will depart today and we will 
continue to assess how we can best assist the people of Vanuatu. Although we are 
currently focused on the immediate relief effort, it is clear that Vanuatu will need long -
term support to recover from this disaster. We already have a significant  aid programme 
in Vanuatu focused on the redevelopment of the port and waterfront infrastructure, and 
we are looking at how we can best support this long-term rebuild.  
There are a number of New Zealanders in Vanuatu, and I know that some families in 
New Zealand are also facing an anxious wait for news. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs 
and Trade consular offices are contacting New Zealanders in Vanuatu to confirm their 
well-being, and at this stage the ministry has not received reports of any New Zealand 
casualties. More than 80 New Zealanders were brought home last night by the Royal 
New Zealand Air Force, and our high commissioner is working to ensure that those who 
do need to leave urgently can do so now that commercial flights have resumed.  
Once again, the thoughts of this House and all New Zealanders are with Vanuatu as 
they confront this calamity, and they can take solace from the fact that they do not stand 
2258 Motions 17 Mar 2015 
 
alone. The international community is rallying, and I can assure the House that New 
Zealand will continue to do all it can to help the relief and recovery efforts. 
ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) : We support the motion. The 
destruction caused by Cyclone Pam has been im mense and heartbreaking, and I would 
like to say how much our hearts go out to the people of Vanuatu, who have suffered 
such a great loss —a loss of life, a loss of homes, a loss of food crops, a loss of those 
things that make up communities, towns, and cit ies. Our sympathies also go out to the 
people of the Solomon Islands and Tuvalu and to the people of the Chatham Islands for 
the tumult they have been through in these last couple of days. To the people of 
Vanuatu, this has been a very hard time for you, a nd in this hard time we in Labour, we 
in this Parliament, we in New Zealand, stand with you in your loss, but we also stand 
with you as you help to rebuild and recover. This has been one of the worst storms to hit 
the Pacific in living memory. The scenes of destruction we have seen and the seemingly 
endless stories of loss will be bringing sadness into the lives of many New Zealanders 
and immense concern and sadness to those from Vanuatu who are on our shores —many 
here for work—who will be anxiously waiting for news.  
But there is little time to mourn. With so much of Vanuatu flattened by this terrible 
event, we need to take action. If we do not, the catastrophe of Cyclone Pam will only 
grow as disease and hunger spread. There is great urgency in our task, but by working 
together with other nations and aid agencies we can ensure that the damage caused by 
the cyclone does not get even worse. That will mean collective effort to bring food, 
medicine, and shelter to those who are hit hardest, and to do it quickly . We will do this 
because we are a family of nations. We are, without doubt, family. We share so much of 
our culture, so much of our heritage, and so many of our people. Now we share loss, but 
with it also the hope that by working together as a family, we can rebuild. In this there 
has been the beginning of hope. The response from the people of New Zealand has been 
swift and generous, as I found out when holding out the bucket up and down Lambton 
Quay just a short while ago. We have been drawn together in t his loss and we will work 
hard to salvage and to rebuild Vanuatu. It will take time because there is a lot to do, and 
we will do it together.

believes is unfair to taxpayers and does not reflect the average wage growth of the wider 
public sector. It is therefore necessary to make amendments to legislation to amend the 
criteria that the Remuneration Authority must consider when setting salaries for 
members of P arliament. The decision to amend the authority’s discretion is not taken 
lightly. However, the change is necessary to ensure that MPs’ remuneration movements 
reflect those in the wider public sector.  
This bill is an omnibus bill that amends two Acts: the Remuneration Authority Act 
1977 and the Members of Parliament (Remuneration and Services) Act 2013. The first 
change is to set aside the part of the Parliamentary Salaries and Allowances 
Determination 2015 that relates to salaries. It then sets out a new r equirement on the 
Remuneration Authority to solely consider public sector wage movements when 
determining the remuneration of MPs.  
The bill does this by pegging MPs’ remuneration to the quarterly employment 
survey, or QES, for the public sector average or dinary-time weekly earnings for 
fulltime-equivalent employees. The quarterly employment survey is a sample survey 
carried out every 3 months by Statistics New Zealand. Each quarter it collects 
information from organisations in the public and private sector s at 18,000 different 
locations. It captures information on hourly earnings, weekly earnings, weekly paid 
hours, and the number of filled jobs. Information from the quarterly employment survey 
is used in the production of Statistics New Zealand’s quarterly  gross domestic product 
and other productivity statistics and for labour market and economic analysis. Changes 
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2275 
 
in quarterly employment survey measures are also used in legislation to benchmark 
figures such as the level of national superannuation and paid parental leave.  
The quarterly employment survey measures actual wage growth, rather than wage 
inflation. Using this means that MPs’ remuneration will increase in line with the 
average public sector salary. Given that the quarterly employment survey measures 
actual wage growth, it is susceptible to potential sudden increases or decreases due to 
fluctuations in employment. As such, the bill also requires that the percentage change 
for each of the reported quarters for any financial year be averaged out to smooth any 
such spikes or dips. Under this bill, the authority will be required, on an annual basis, to 
adjust MPs’ remuneration by the quarterly employment survey public sector index, 
using the June rate from the previous year measured against the current ye ar. For the 
June 2014 year, the quarterly employment survey public sector increase was 1.5 
percent.  
The bill will make a minor change to the formula for determining MPs’ 
remuneration. The authority will be required to take the previous year’s base salary and 
superannuation and multiply this by the quarterly employment survey index. This figure 
will be the remuneration for the current year. The authority will be required to adjust 
remuneration to take account of personal benefits where there is a change to the level of 
an existing entitlement provided. A recent example of this is in the 2015 determination, 
where the Remuneration Authority reduced the value of the travel entitlement to 
account for tightened provisions around the use of travel by family member s. In this 
scenario the reduction in personal benefit created as the result of that tightened 
provision will be shifted to the cash component of the remuneration—that is, base 
salary. It will not be subject to the quarterly employment survey adjustment in the first 
year in which it is transferred. There are no changes to how the authority, the Speaker of 
the House, and the Minister responsible for Ministerial Services determine the value of 
personal benefits for MPs and their families, such as travel. These  changes will also not 
affect any of the persons that the Remuneration Authority determines remuneration for 
other than MPs.  
Although the current practice of the authority is to gazette a determination for 
parliamentary salaries and allowances on an annual basis, it is required to do so only 
every 3 years. The bill requires that the authority must fix MPs’ salaries on an annual 
basis to ensure salaries stay in line with annual changes in public sector wages.  
The MPs’ salary determination that was issued b y the Remuneration Authority on 26 
February 2015 will be revoked, apart from the provisions in this determination that 
relate to allowances, which stay in place. The authority gazetted its determination for 
the 2014-15 financial year based on existing stat utory criteria. So that the new criterion 
applies to salary adjustments from 1 July 2014, the bill revokes and overwrites the 
effect of the 2015 determination for salaries. The provision relating to allowances will 
remain in effect. The 2013 determination will come back into force until the authority is 
able to gazette a new determination for the period of 1 July 2014 to 30 June 2015 based 
on the amendments Parliament has made to the Act. Any changes in salaries resulting 
from the new determination will be backdated to 1 July 2014.  
This bill responds to the disproportionate growth in MPs’ total remuneration by 
providing a sensible measure that reflects the average growth in public sector wages. I 
commend this bill to the House.

Dr PARMJEET PARMAR (National) : It is great to be able to speak on and 
support the Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament Remuneration) 
Amendment Bill. First, I would like to congratulate the Minister in charge, the Hon 
Michael Woodhouse, on the work that he has done on this bill in such a short time. The 
Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill, 
sponsored by the Hon Michael Woodhouse, is to amend the Remuneration Authorit y 
Act 1977. This bill is going through all stages today under urgency. This is because the 
latest increase, which was determined by the Remuneration Authority, was to increase 
the salary of members of Parliament by 3.56 percent. Although this decision was made 
independently of members of Parliament, we should not be receiving this increase 
because it is disproportionate to increases in the public sector.  
When this issue was raised by the Prime Minister the Remuneration Authority 
referred to a specific criterion in the Remuneration Authority Act 1977 as the reason for 
this increase, and that is why this change is necessary. This change will tie the salaries 
of members of Parliament to the public sector and will take away the Remuneration 
Authority’s discretion when setting the salaries of members of Parliament. Given that 
inflation is 0.8 percent this kind of increase is not necessary. I am really proud to be part 
of this team that believes in delivering for our Kiwi families and children. We are taking 
action; it is not just about talking —like the Greens we heard. This is not a new issue. 
This is not an issue that is raised for the first time. It is about fairness for the taxpayer’s 
dollar.  
The amendment will change the process of how the Remuneration Author ity reviews 
the salaries of members of Parliament. So, first, it will take away the Remuneration 
Authority’s discretion when setting the salaries of members of Parliament. Second, it 
will make the average public sector pay movement the sole criterion for d etermining 
increases in the salaries of members of Parliament. This will be backdated to 1 July 
2014. This amendment will mean that the average annual percentage change in public 
sector pay, as measured by Statistics New Zealand’s quarterly employment surv ey, will 
be used to determine a member of Parliament’s salary. Using the quarterly employment 
survey will mean that the increases that members of Parliament will get will be in line 
with the wider public sector. The law change will be backdated to 1 July 2014, which 
means that the determination of 3.56 percent of the Remuneration Authority will not be 
awarded. This increase will be somewhere around 1.5 percent.  
Currently, the Remuneration Authority has to take into account several factors, such 
as relativity to comparable positions and the requirements of the job. With this change 
the authority will just need to annually apply the average quarterly employment survey 
index for the June year to give an increase to members of Parliament. The 
2290 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015 
 
Remuneration Authority will continue to have the ability to change the mix of cash and 
non-cash items in the overall pay package. This indexing of the salaries of members of 
Parliament to the quarterly employment survey will be done at the same time every 
year. This is afte r the publication of the quarterly employment survey in June every 
year. This will make sure that the increases we get are in line with those our teachers, 
nurses, and other workers get.

National-led Government are about. Pay and pay increases, I understand,  are rewards

and they are dedicated. But we are not here for the financial reward.  I am here to serve 
our people; I am here to serve our country. So I am really honoured to be part of this 
team that believes in delivering more for less. It is about listening to our people and it is 
about being fair to our people, so I support this bill.

Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and 
Safety): I move, That the Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament 
Remuneration) Amendment Bill be now read a third time . The bill is the Government’s 
response to the most recent determination of the Remuneration Authority, which 
provides for an increase in the remuneration received by MPs of 3.56 percent, effective 
from 1 July 2014. The Government considers this increase to be disproportionate to the 
salary movements in the wider public sector and unfair to taxpayers. The bill limits the 
Remuneration Authority consideration to applying the wage growth in the public sector, 
as measured by the quarterly employment survey, to MPs’ remuneration. The bill 
provides a fair response to the disproportionate increase in MPs’ remuneration by 
17 Mar 2015 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 2333 
 
providing a measure that reflects the average growth in public sector wages. This 
ensures that the taxpayer is not unfairly burdened by any unwarranted increases in 
remuneration. In summation, the Government believes that these alignments will align 
MPs’ remuneration with that of the wider public sector and will strike the right balance 
between the interests of taxpayers and those whose remuneration is being assessed. I 
commend the bill to the House. 
CHRIS HIPKINS (Labour —Rimutaka): That was a slightly shorter contribution 
from the Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety, Michael Woodhouse, than I was 
anticipating. I am happy to rise to do my final contribution in this debate on the 
Remuneration Authority (Members of Parliament Remuneration) Amendment Bill. I 
want to just first of all say that the mechanism that this House establishes for 
determining how MPs’ pay s hould be set is a very important one constitutionally. It is 
not good practice for Parliament itself to be voting on, debating, and setting, effectively, 
what the taxpayer should pay us for doing this job. It is important that we put in place a 
robust mechanism that removes those decisions from this House and places them with 
an independent body that can make those decisions rigorously and independently.  
I think the public of New Zealand would like to have that reassurance that in fact we 
are not here feat hering our own nests and debating things that are going to be in our 
own best interests and that there is someone independent making decisions about what a 
fair rate of pay for members of Parliament should be. This is, in fact, an important issue. 
No one here is arguing for a significant pay increase at the moment, but ensuring that 
MPs receive a sufficient and appropriate level of remuneration is actually important for 
the transparency and integrity of the democratic system of government. It is actually one 
of the guards that we have against corruption. Making sure that MPs are appropriately 
remunerated for the job that we do is one of the ways that the public of New Zealand 
and the taxpayer can have the reassurance that we are working for them and not for 
other people who are paying us and giving us money for the work that we do. The only 
way that the public can have the assurance that that is what is happening is when those 
decisions are made completely independently of this House and when there are robust  
criteria for doing so.  
It has been apparent for some time now that there were issues with the criteria that 
the Remuneration Authority had in determining what MPs’ pay should be, and it is high 
time that the House resolved those issues. This is not a good process for doing that. We 
have had 5 years of concerns. We have had 5 years where the criteria could have been 
properly and appropriately amended without the need to resort to urgency. It is, 
therefore, unfortunate that we now find ourselves in this pos ition where if we do not 
conclude this debate this week under urgency —through all of the bill’s stages —then 
MPs will get the significant pay increases next week that we are here tonight trying to 
stop from happening. That could have been avoided if this ha d been dealt with through 
a much better, more rigorous, and proper process. Unfortunately, that has not happened, 
and therefore urgency is the only way now to stop those pay rises going through and 
being in MPs’ bank accounts next week.  
We on the Labour P arty side have listened very carefully to the debate and we have 
engaged with it in good faith, with the principle being that we wanted to stop those rises 
going through and we wanted to make sure that the criteria are amended in a way that is 
robust and that will provide an enduring and independent solution for how MPs’ pay is 
set. That is the reason that we voted in favour of the legislation and in favour of 
urgency, because without urgency, as I have said, there would have been no way to stop 
those pay increases.  
However, having listened to the debate, we did vote in favour of Supplementary 
Order Paper 58 put forward by Metiria Turei, which would have resulted in the 
2334 Remuneration Authority (MPs Remuneration) Amdt Bill 17 Mar 2015 
 
legislation being passed now but stopping only those pay increases, and leaving for 
another day the decision around what the new criteria should be, because we do not 
think that this is a good process. We would rather that it went through a more rigorous 
process, particularly, and this is a big issue for me because I would like to ensure that  
the Remuneration Authority —the experts on this; the people who have to actually 
implement it—is able to provide some scrutiny of the legislation that we are now 
passing. It has not had the opportunity to do so and it will not have the opportunity to do 
so. As a result we cannot be sure that the legislation that we are passing now is actually 
going to do what it purports to do in the short term and in the long term. There is a 
possibility that in the long term this will give us bigger pay increases than the  existing 
criteria that we have, which we are now replacing. That is one of the reasons there needs 
to be greater scrutiny of these matters —so that we can be sure that the bill does what it 
is supposed to do. We do not have that because of the way this process has been rushed.  
One of the concerning things that became very apparent during the debate is that this 
debate is, in fact, only partly about MPs’ pay and that, actually, the wider agenda from 
the Government is to suppress the pay overall across the w hole of the public sector, 
including teachers, doctors, nurses, police, prison officers, and so on—we could go on 
and on through all of the professions. It is very disappointing to hear members from the 
National Party referring to those who work for the good of the public and who want pay 
increases as union thugs. I think that is very disappointing. I think that after a long 
period of time when their pay rises have not kept up with inflation—in fact, in real 
terms their salaries have gone backwards —it is fa ir enough that they are asking for a 
pay increase. 
I heard Bill English claiming —I think it was either today or yesterday —that, in fact, 
teachers, for example, have had pay rises above inflation. So I went and looked at the 
top of the teacher salary scale.  These are the most experienced teachers, the longest -
serving—teachers, the ones who do not have any other management roles or whatever 
and who are just simply at the top of the teacher salary scale. Here are the real numbers: 
in 2009 they were paid $68,980 and as of last year they were paid $72,646. So let us be 
clear. These are the most experienced teachers. That is a 5.3 percent pay increase. What 
did inflation do during that time? It was 9.3 percent during that time. Actually, in real 
terms, a teacher w ho has no management responsibilities and who is at the top of the 
salary scale has gone backwards in the last 4 or 5 years under this National 
Government, and yet Bill English is saying that they should not be getting any pay 
increase at all. They have seen the real value of their incomes eroded during that time.  
So the Government is up against the wall this year when a lot of these big public 
sector collective agreements come up for negotiation because actually people have been 
promised for 5 years by this Government —and maybe longer —that there will be jam 
tomorrow, but jam never actually comes, and they are saying that they have had enough 
of that. I think that is quite understandable. I think it is wrong that the Government uses 
this debate on MPs’ pay to try to suppress the debate over wider pay issues within the 
public sector. I do not think MPs should be getting significant pay increases of the 
magnitude that were recently awarded, but I actually do think it is probably time to look 
at some of those pay rates in the public sector because there has been a lot of belt 
tightening.  
Finally, I just want to make one last contribution in this debate, and that is around the 
actual formula that this bill is now establishing, which links MP pay increases to the  
average increases within the public sector. As I have raised during earlier parts of this 
debate, that can create some unintended consequences because the overall average 
increase in the public sector can be distorted by higher -than-average increases in 
managerial salaries for those at the top of the salary scale and lower increases for those

who are on regular and low incomes. As a result, our pay will go up while the pay of the
